Inbound Call Handling / Inbound Lead Closing

This SOP covers what happens when a live call lands in your queue at app.krestmarketing.com — from the moment you pick up through pushing the prospect's data to the correct backend and starting the soft credit pull.

Where these calls come from

Every lead source below is a different campaign type agents get assigned to. The Narrative column is the story the prospect has in their head when they pick up — know it before you say hello, since it's what tells you how to flip or sell them.

Before logging in each day — or at various points during the day — agents will know which lead type they're assigned to. Check your assignment against this table first, so you already have the right narrative in mind before your first call of that block comes in, rather than figuring it out call by call.

Glossary

Terms used in the table above, explained in full. Click a term to expand it.

The standard value proposition for prospects responding to a hardship-loan or pre-qualification offer (Inbound Routed Vendor Calls): they called in expecting a new loan, and the pitch repositions our program as the better path instead of a like-for-like loan. Needs input from your team: the actual script content itself isn't documented here yet.
Leads who opted in while completing an unrelated online form or survey — a sweepstakes entry, a financial calculator, an insurance quote request — that included a checkbox agreeing to be contacted about relevant offers. If asked "how did you get my info?", tell them plainly: they completed an online survey that included consent to be contacted.
A business process outsourcing partner's live agent stays on the line and verbally introduces the prospect directly to us, rather than a blind/cold transfer. Confirm what they were already told before you start qualifying.
A voicemail dropped directly into a prospect's mailbox without their phone ever ringing. It's what many Inbound Routed Vendor Calls and In-House RVM/SMS prospects are responding to when they call back.
Debt Threshold is the minimum debt level typically seen on that source. (Targeted) means the campaign is aimed at prospects around that debt level, not a guaranteed floor every caller meets. Avg. Debt is an observed range rather than a minimum.
How long you have to qualify the prospect before the call vendor bills us for that call — it's a cost window, not just a scheduling gap. "None" means the source isn't billed against a live call window (spooled or self-initiated calls). Full guidance on working inside it is on the Qualifying Efficiently tab.

Legal requirement · non-negotiable

DNC / DND Compliance

We are required by federal law — the TCPA (Telephone Consumer Protection Act) — to honor every Do Not Call request. This isn't a courtesy or a nice-to-have. It's the law, and it applies to every single call, every single time.

This is critical to the company's legal survival TCPA violations carry statutory penalties per violation, and can be tripled for willful violations. This exposure is real, not theoretical — companies in this exact industry have faced serious class-action lawsuits over failure to honor DNC requests. Every agent honoring every request, every time, without exception, is what keeps the company protected.

What counts as a DNC request

Treat all of these identically — there's no magic phrase required. If a prospect says anything like this, it's a DNC request:

  • “Put me on your do not call list”
  • “Stop calling me”
  • “Remove my number”
  • “Take me off your list”
  • “Don't call again”

What to do the moment you hear it

Acknowledge immediately

Don't argue, don't ask why, and don't try to re-pitch or salvage the call. The request stands the instant it's made.

Confirm you're processing it

A simple, direct confirmation is enough — something like "Understood, I'll take care of that right now." No further sales conversation after this point.

Mark it in the system

There are two ways to DND a contact in app.krestmarketing.com. Use whichever is documented below — more steps and the second method are still being added.

Method 1: Tagging Step 1 — open the contact record and click into the Tags field (or the tag icon next to the phone number) to open Add tag(s).
Contact Details — opening Add tag(s) from the Tags field
Method 1: Tagging — Step 2 Search “dnd” in the tag search box, select dnd/do not call/do not disturb, then click Apply.
Select tags — searching, selecting, and applying the dnd/do not call/do not disturb tag
Method 2: Mark DND Directly On the contact record, click the DND tab (next to All fields and Actions). Check DND All Channels to block everything at once — or check individual channels (Email, Text Messages, Calls & voicemail, Inbound Calls and SMS) if only some need to be blocked. This takes effect immediately; the conversation log will confirm with a note like “DnD enabled by user for SMS, Email and Call.”
Contact record — the DND tab, with DND All Channels and per-channel toggles, and the conversation log confirming it took effect
The two methods are connected Applying the dnd/do not call/do not disturb tag (Method 1) is meant to trigger a backend workflow that sets these same DND channel toggles automatically — so tagging and toggling directly both land on the same result. Method 2 is the more direct route if you want to confirm it landed, or to block only specific channels rather than everything.

End the call professionally

Thank them for their time and end the call. No follow-up call, text, or email after a DNC request — on this number, from any campaign.

How this flows through our systems

DNC is treated as source-agnostic — once a number is flagged, it stays suppressed regardless of which campaign or lead source it originally came from. The Funding Tier CRM consolidates call disposition, the DNC tag, and the manual DND toggle into a single Contact DND state. The moment that's set, an automated workflow fires that suppresses the number in TrackDrive as well (caller_remove + opt_out=true) — so marking it correctly in the CRM is what actually keeps that person from being called again by any system downstream.

One nuance: already-enrolled clients An active, enrolled client is not marked DND in The Funding Tier CRM even if they ask to stop marketing contact — they still need to receive servicing communications (billing, account updates). Their suppression from further marketing happens on the TrackDrive side only. This nuance mostly matters for backend/servicing teams, not for a live inbound qualification call, but it's worth knowing so you're not confused if an enrolled client's record doesn't show DND set in the CRM.
Working the call

Qualifying Efficiently Within Buffer Time

Every lead source on the Overview tab carries its own buffer time — the window you have to qualify a prospect before the call vendor bills us for it. Qualifying fast and well inside that window is its own skill, separate from knowing which fields to fill in.

What "buffer time" actually means It's how long you have to qualify the prospect before the call vendor bills us for that call. It's not about call cadence — it's about cost. Qualify slowly, or fail to qualify at all inside the window, and you've spent both the vendor's fee and your own time on nothing. Getting to a clear qualify/disqualify decision quickly is what buffer time is actually protecting.

Working efficiently

Front-load the disqualifiers

Get to unsecured debt amount, employment, and monthly payment history early — these tell you fastest whether this is a real opportunity. Don't spend buffer time building rapport on a call that's going to disqualify anyway.

Know your script cold

Hesitating over what to ask next is the single biggest buffer-time killer. The qualification order on the Qualification Questions tab is fixed for a reason — run it the same way every time so you're not thinking, just executing.

Confirm, don't re-ask, what's already known

Phone number, and anything already captured upstream (see the "check before you re-type" note on the backend SOPs), gets confirmed in a sentence, not re-collected from scratch.

Reading deal quality on lower-debt files

$4,000 is a floor, not a target Technically, a prospect can be enrolled with as little as $4,000 in eligible debt (Consumer Shield's minimum). That doesn't mean every file at that level is a good deal. Watch for this pattern: someone whose accounts are fully utilized (maxed out) at a low dollar amount often has a low credit limit, which correlates with lower income — and lower income is exactly what puts ability to pay for the program itself at risk.

What to weigh, not just the debt total

Use the same qualification answers you're already collecting: employment status and the total they already pay each month toward debts. Someone with $4-5K in debt who's fully maxed out and has little room in their monthly budget is a materially weaker file than someone with the same debt total who simply hasn't used much of their available credit. Debt size alone doesn't tell you the story — ability to pay does.

Verifying income & source of funds

This is what actually confirms deal quality, and it's also required to complete the client's budget analysis. Don't stop at "are they employed?" — get the specific numbers.

If employed

Ask how much they take home after each paycheck, not just their job title or salary range. Also ask if they have any additional sources of funds beyond their paycheck — a second job, a side income, support from a partner.

If not employed

Ask whether they have another source of funds: retirement income, Social Security, disability, or similar. Someone can still be a legitimate file without a job, as long as there's a real, steady source of money behind it.

No job and no source of funds is a real red flag If a prospect has no employment income and no other source of funds, something isn't right — they won't qualify for a loan or a relief program unless they have savings they're able to draw on to pay. Don't just check the "employed?" box and move on; if the answer is no, always follow up with what money they actually have coming in.

Vetting the call against the full qualification script

The questions on this page cover data entry order. For the complete qualification methodology — how to vet and qualify a call across all three programs — use the script at ai.fundingtier.com/agents/call-scripts alongside this page, not instead of it.

Watch for vendor-coached debt figures — this is critical Some paid lead vendors are financially incentivized to coach prospects into overstating their debt, since a bigger reported number can make a lead look more qualified and worth more to the vendor. An enrollment built on an inflated number doesn't survive contact with the soft credit pull — and by the time that pull happens, the file has already been pushed to a backend as if it were solid. Catching this at the call is the only point where it's cheap to catch.

Signs a figure may be coached, not real

  • The prospect gives one clean total but can't break it down by individual creditor or account when asked
  • The number lands suspiciously exactly on a program threshold (e.g. precisely $10,000, not "somewhere around")
  • Hesitation, a pause to "check," or a scripted-sounding answer when you ask a natural follow-up they shouldn't need to be coached on
  • The debt story doesn't match the narrative for that lead source (see the Overview table) — e.g. someone who came in on a source with a low typical debt suddenly reporting a number at the top of another program's range

What to do about it

Ask them to walk you through it creditor by creditor rather than accepting one lump figure — a real number is easy to break down; a coached one usually isn't. If the breakdown doesn't add up to what they first told you, go with what they can actually substantiate, not the headline number.

Apply this tag: “coached / suspicious warm transfer” When you suspect coaching, apply coached / suspicious warm transfer in The Funding Tier CRM (app.krestmarketing.com). That tag routes the call into review and vendor escalation, rather than you deciding case-by-case whether to enroll at a lower number or drop the file. The specific lead vendor is identified automatically — a separate workflow already running in coordination with TrackDrive attaches it, so you don't need to note which vendor it came from yourself.

The complete required-fields reference

Confirmed directly from the live contact record. These two screenshots are the source of truth for what's required — both videos above walk through entering them live.

Contact Details (1/4) — First Name, Last Name, Cell Phone, Phone, Email, Street Address, City, State, and Postal Code are all required
Contact Details, continued — Marital Status, Date of Birth, Social Security Number, and Country are also required
Already known · required

Cell Phone & Phone

You already have this from the call transfer. Read it back to the prospect to confirm it's correct and reachable — don't re-ask for it as if it's new information. Both the Cell Phone and Phone fields are required.

Required

First Name & Last Name

Get the full legal name, spelled if it's unusual. This is what will appear on every downstream document.

Required

Email Address

Read it back letter by letter, including the domain, before moving on.

Required

Street Address

Full mailing address — street number, street name, apartment/unit if applicable.

Required

City

Full city name, matching the street address given.

Required · system fix required

State

Always select the state from the dropdown list — never type it in freehand.

Why this matters Typing a state in as free text (e.g. typing "CA" into an open field instead of picking California from the list) breaks state-based eligibility and compliance logic downstream, since those systems match against the dropdown's stored values, not arbitrary text. Always click the field and choose the state from the list that appears.
Required

Postal Code

Full 5-digit ZIP code. Confirm it matches the state selected above.

Required · pre-populated

Country

Defaults to United States already — you don't need to ask for it or set it manually. It's still a required field, just one that's already filled in for you. Leave it as-is unless the prospect specifically isn't a US resident.

Marital Status, Date of Birth, and SSN are also required These three don't live on this tab — Marital Status is covered on Qualification Questions, and Date of Birth & SSN are covered on SSN Collection. All three are just as required as everything above; the push and soft credit pull need the complete set.
Step 2

Collecting the Social Security Number

The SSN is required to run the soft credit pull. Some prospects are uncomfortable saying it out loud on a phone call — that's expected, and there's a workaround for it.

Why we need it The SSN is what lets the backend (Level Debt, ELP, or Consumer Shield) pull the prospect's credit report and verify their identity in the Soft Credit Pull & Verification step. Without it, the file can't move past qualification — there's no way to confirm the debts the prospect described or run identity verification.
Standard path

Ask directly

Ask for the SSN and enter it into the SSN field on the contact record. Read the last four digits back to confirm before moving on.

Optional · workaround

SSN Secure Form Collector

If the prospect doesn't want to say their SSN out loud, don't push them to say it — use the SSN Secure Form Collector instead. It generates a one-time authentication link and sends it to the prospect by SMS (and optionally email, whichever they confirm they can access right now, while you stay on the line). They open the link to an enterprise-style page and enter exactly nine digits, which are validated before they can submit.

Using the SSN Secure Form CollectorScreen recording
What happens after they submit The link shows as used once they've submitted (or expired if they don't). The system records the last four digits, a consent timestamp, IP address and user-agent as proof of submission, and a secure vault record ID for encrypted/hashed storage of the full number. Once verified, that SSN is what's used to run the soft credit pull.
What to say when you send the link Stay on the line and tell them plainly: “You will receive a secure, personalized page for entry — let me know once that's completed so we can get you verified.” Wait for their verbal confirmation before moving on, rather than sending it and following up after the call.
How to confirm it went through Refresh the contact screen — once the prospect completes the form, the SSN appears directly on the contact record. That's your confirmation it worked.
Step 3

Pushing the File to a Backend

Applying one of the tags below is a single action that does two things at once: it pushes the contact to the matching backend, and that push is what triggers the soft credit pull. It's not two separate mechanisms — it's one tag, applied at the right moment.

Video walkthrough The screen recording on the Contact Info Capture tab covers entering the contact record and pushing it to a backend, start to finish — watch it there for the full sequence.
Apply the tag early, not at the end of the call Don't wait until the full qualification conversation (step 4) is finished to tag the lead. Apply the tag as soon as name, DOB, SSN, marital status, and phone are captured — right after step 2 — so the credit pull starts as early as possible. Whatever qualification answers you gather afterward still need to make it into the backend; see the note below.
Required fields — the push won't fire correctly without these Confirmed from the live contact record: First Name, Last Name, Cell Phone, Phone, Email, Street Address, City, State, Postal Code, Country, Marital Status, Date of Birth, and Social Security Number are all required before you tag. Don't apply the tag with any of these still blank — see the Contact Info Capture tab for the full annotated reference.
Confirmed: qualification answers don't need to sync anywhere The Qualification Questions (Estimated Unsecured Debt, Total Monthly Payment, Employment Status) don't go to, or matter to, the backend at all — they're purely for your own read on the prospect, not data the push or the backend systems use. There's nothing to enter into Forth/Salesforce/Consumer Shield separately after tagging; the only fields that matter downstream are the required ones above.

How tagging works

Open Select tags on the contact record, search, and apply the one tag that matches where this file is going. Applying the tag is what fires the webhook — nothing pushes until the tag is added.

Available push tags

push to elp + level – (forth + sales force) push to consumer shield push to forth crm | level push to legacy / elp / sales force
Only apply one push tag Each tag routes the file to a different destination system (or combination of systems). Applying the wrong one — or more than one — sends the prospect's data somewhere it doesn't belong. Confirm the program from the qualification questions before tagging.
This is why accuracy here matters Applying the tag pushes everything you entered — name, phone, email, address, DOB, SSN, qualification answers — directly into the backend (Forth, Salesforce, or Consumer Shield's system) via webhook. The agent enrolling this file on the backend side should not need to re-type any of it; they're instructed to check that it came through correctly rather than re-enter it from scratch. A mistake made here is a mistake that follows the file everywhere it goes next.

Which backend to push to

Debt Settlement (Level Debt) is the default

Which backend(s) you push to depends on which program you're actually enrolling this prospect into — and that in turn is what decides which system runs the soft credit pull. Debt Settlement via Level Debt is the default whenever the prospect is eligible for it.

Eligible debtPrograms available
$4,000–$5,999Consumer Shield only
$6,000–$6,999ELP or Consumer Shield
$7,000+All three programs available — default to Level Debt

When it's NOT Level Debt

  • Eligible debt is under $7,000 — Level Debt isn't available yet; route per the table above ($4K–$5,999 Consumer Shield only, $6K–$6,999 ELP or Consumer Shield)
  • The client elects to pursue the resolution program (ELP) after you've explained the options and the differences between them — their choice overrides the default
  • They're already enrolled in a debt settlement program elsewhere and want something cheaper — ELP and Consumer Shield/Shield Services are both cheaper alternatives to offer
Simulate it yourself You can run the router logic on a sample debt load — try $10K, $20K, and $30K — in the AI Deal Router tool to see exactly how it resolves in practice.
Confirmed: what “Forth” and “Sales Force” mean Within the push tags (e.g. push to elp + level – (forth + sales force)), Forth = Level Debt and Sales Force = ELP. Those are the two backend systems the tag pushes the contact into, named after the underlying platforms each program runs on.
Needs input from your team Still open: any state-specific restrictions that affect this routing beyond debt amount.
Step 4

Qualification Questions

Asked after the backend push (previous tab) — the credit pull is already running by this point. These questions matter for reading the prospect, not for the backend. Know why you're asking, not just what to ask.

Video walkthrough The screen recording on the Contact Info Capture tab is the extended version — it also covers this qualification step, alongside contact entry and the backend push, start to finish.
Two different kinds of fields here Marital Status, DOB, and SSN are hard requirements — the push won't fire without them (see Pushing to Backends). Estimated Unsecured Debt, Total Monthly Payment, and Employment Status are used differently: they don't go to, or matter to, the backend at all. They're a qualitative read, purely for you as the agent to form a mental judgment on whether this prospect is actually likely to enroll — not data that needs to be entered, pushed, or synced anywhere.
The actual contact record fields in app.krestmarketing.com — Estimated Amount of Unsecured Debt, Total Amount Paid Each Month, Are You Currently Employed, Marital Status, Date of birth, and Social Security Number, all highlighted
Country is pre-populated The Country field defaults to United States already — you don't need to ask for it or set it manually. Leave it as-is unless the prospect specifically isn't a US resident.
Qualitative · sizes the opportunity

Estimated Amount of Unsecured Debt

This gives you a read on the size of the opportunity and which program(s) the prospect can even qualify for.

Always confirm the debt is actually unsecured Most people don't know what "unsecured" means, so don't just ask "how much unsecured debt do you have" and take the number at face value — walk them through it. Unsecured debt is things like credit cards, personal loans, medical bills, and collections. It is not a student loan, a car loan, or a solar panel loan — those are secured or otherwise excluded and will throw off eligibility if counted in the total.
Qualitative · ability & willingness to pay

Total Amount Paid Each Month Towards Debts

This isn't just a data point — it's your read on whether this prospect actually pays their bills. Someone who has a track record of making monthly payments toward their debt is a much better bet to keep paying once they're in a program. If they're already behind on everything, that's a signal worth noting, not ignoring.

Qualitative · ability to pay

Are You Currently Employed?

Employment is the most direct signal of whether the prospect can actually afford the program payment going forward. Get a clear yes/no, and if relevant, what kind of income (job, self-employed, fixed income) it is.

Why it matters · required before you can push

Marital Status

Marital status affects how the application and enrollment are structured. If the prospect is married, always follow up with the next question — don't skip it.

Capture this before you tag, not here Marital Status is a required field for the push — along with DOB and SSN, it needs to be on the contact record before you apply the tag (see the Overview flow and Pushing to Backends tab). Get it during identity capture, not saved for later in this qualification conversation.
If married: are the debts joint or individual? Ask whether the enrolled debts are in joint accounts (both spouses' names) or only in the prospect's name. This changes who's liable for the debt and needs to be captured accurately — don't assume either way.
Non-negotiable · required for every program

Date of Birth & Social Security Number

Both must be entered correctly — the soft credit pull will fail or return the wrong person's data if either is off by even one digit. Read both back to the prospect to confirm before moving on.

This applies to every program, no exceptions Level Debt, Elite Legal Practice, and Consumer Shield all require an accurate DOB and SSN to run their soft credit pull. There is no program where you can skip or approximate these fields. See the SSN Collection tab if the prospect doesn't want to say their SSN out loud.
Step 5

Soft Credit Pull & Identity Verification

Once the file has been pushed to the backend, that system is what runs the credit pull and identity check — not app.krestmarketing.com itself.

What a soft credit pull is

A soft credit pull (also called a "soft inquiry") checks a prospect's credit report and score without affecting their credit score and without appearing to other lenders as an inquiry. It's used here purely to confirm eligibility and pull in the debt/creditor information needed to build the program — not to make a lending decision. This is different from a "hard pull," which does affect credit score and is typically only used when a lender is extending new credit.

Explaining it to the prospect

If they ask what this means for their credit: a soft pull does not lower their score, does not show up to other lenders, and is not the same as applying for a new loan or credit card. It's simply how we confirm the debt information they've already told us about.

On a loan swap call specifically

When the prospect is responding to a hardship loan or pre-qualification offer (Inbound Routed Vendor Calls — see the Loan Flip / Loan Swap glossary entry on Overview), frame the pull as something we're required to do, not optional: “We're required to verify eligibility for all personal loans, offers, or alternative programs. There's no effect to your score, and you can also get a free copy of your report to review as well.”

Verifying identity

Primary · Spinwheel (via Forth)

Forth's built-in Spinwheel integration verifies identity automatically as part of running the credit pull, using the contact information already on file.

Fallback · KBA

If Spinwheel can't confirm identity automatically, fall back to Knowledge-Based Authentication (KBA) — a short set of multiple-choice questions pulled from the prospect's credit history (e.g. past addresses or loans) that only the real person should be able to answer.
